en: On 14 April, Ambedkar Jayanti, you marched with the neighbourhood. Children carried his picture at the front.
{0} told you about the day in 1956 in Nagpur when hundreds of thousands became Buddhists together with Dr Ambedkar.
A friend from another caste took you into the family kitchen, and the two of you ate from one plate.
{0} was proud of the skill of {1}, who had worked as a smith. Every sickle and hoe in the village, she said, had passed through his hands.
In the village's Dalit youth group you learned to read and write together, and how to report discrimination.
Every evening you gathered the neighbourhood children and taught them. That was how you had learned too.
You were the first in the family to earn a university degree. Your parents hung the graduation photo where everyone would see it.

On Christmas night, the neighbourhood gathered in the small church to sing and share food.
You grew up speaking {0} at home and Nepali at school. Moving between the two came naturally.
For a few hours a week at school you learned from textbooks in {0}. It felt strange and wonderful to see the language of home in a book.
You sang a lullaby in {0} to your grandchild, who clumsily sang along.
{0} gave the woman who came to work at the house a cup kept apart. You poured her tea in your own cup.
{0} told a neighbour not to step over the threshold. You invited the neighbour into the house.
When a friend could not rent a room because of caste, you went along to see the landlord together.
You told your child not to ask friends their caste: people are not divided by such things.
About 5% of married women in India married across castes (India Human Development Survey IHDS-II 2011-12)
With the change of faith, the places set aside for Scheduled Castes were no longer yours.
In India only Hindus, Sikhs and Buddhists are counted as Scheduled Castes (Presidential Order of 1950, amended 1956 and 1990)
About 5.3% of American children spend time in foster care before 18. Of children leaving care, 46% go home and 26% are adopted (Yi et al. 2020; US HHS AFCARS 2025)
About 4% of children born in England in 2000 were looked after before 18 (Jay et al. 2022). Of children leaving care in 2025, about 9% were adopted (UK Department for Education)
Of children born in New Zealand in 1998, 3.1% were placed out of home before 18, and 7.1% of Māori children (Rouland & Vaithianathan 2018)
First Nations children in Australia are in out-of-home care about 11 times as often as other children (AIHW 2024)
In 2023, 2,054 children in need of protection in Korea were placed in a facility or with a family; about 90% of family foster care is with grandparents and relatives (Ministry of Health and Welfare)
About 42,000 children in Japan are in alternative care, and about a quarter of them grow up in foster families (MHLW; Children and Families Agency)

Since the 1950s about 170,000 Korean children have been adopted abroad, about 65% to the United States. In the 1970s and 1980s it was about 1 in every 100 babies born (Ministry of Health and Welfare, AP 2025)
Since 1992 about 160,000 Chinese children have been adopted abroad, most of them girls. China ended adoptions abroad in 2024
In 2007 about 1 in every 100 babies born in Guatemala was adopted abroad, nearly all to the United States. Forged papers and the buying of babies came to light, and adoptions abroad stopped in 2008
From 1999 to 2012 about 60,000 Russian children were adopted by families in the United States. Russia barred adoptions by Americans in 2013
After the 1989 revolution showed the world Romania's orphanages, more than 10,000 children were adopted abroad in 1990-91 alone. Romania stopped adoptions abroad in 2001
Around 2010 Ethiopia sent more than 4,000 children a year abroad for adoption, and banned adoptions abroad in 2018
Adoptions across borders peaked at about 45,000 in 2004 and have fallen steeply since (Selman, Hague Conference on Private International Law)
